The message to developers is that land, power, and a finished building matter more than a pitch deck. ⁠Anita Verma-Lallian⁠ has been selling exactly that. Her company, Arizona Land Consulting, assembles data center sites for developers, hyperscalers, AI labs, and neoclouds, giving her a view into who’s buying, what makes a site viable, and where projects are running into trouble. She also partners with investor ⁠Chamath Palihapitiya,⁠ who has been predicting an industry shakeout. On this episode of TechCrunch’s ⁠Equity⁠ podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Verma-Lallian about who bears the risk when Nvidia gets pickier, why speculative projects could be the first to fall apart, and what a 2027 shakeout might look like. Listen to the full episode to hear more about: What “land, power, shell” means, and why having all three could give some developers a major advantage. How community opposition and state-level restrictions are making some markets harder to build in than others. Utilities getting major customers like TSMC to help fund the infrastructure needed to deliver more power. Who gets stuck with the bill when a data center project stalls, from developers to lenders to customers. Why AI labs and hyperscalers might increasingly build their own data centers instead of relying on neoclouds. Who could benefit from a 2027 shakeout, including the companies best positioned to acquire distressed projects. content:
Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000 Published November 25, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 4 Niels Rogge nielsr Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here . One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs ( sm100 ), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ. We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint . Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs , and let it run experiments for an afternoon. Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb . The setup The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script ( bench.py ): Measure the hardware and estimate theoretical ceilings before tuning. Change one variable at a time and bracket every candidate between two control runs ( control → candidate → control ). Keep a change only if it beats both controls without regressing other metrics. Log every run in PLAN.md , including regressions and dead ends. Pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks before declaring a winner. bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled. The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure: HF Jobs for compute. The rtx-pro-6000 Job flavor uses the same GPU as the nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint ($2.75/h for both), so Job numbers transfer directly. A ~150-line driver ( jobs/driver.py ) takes a list of server configs, starts each one, runs an unmeasured warmup, calls bench.py unmodified, shuts the server down, and prints one ledger line per run. Because Jobs run on separate machines, the agent swept SGLang ( lmsysorg/sglang:inkling-2-mini ) and vLLM nightly ( vllm/vllm-openai:nightly ) in parallel. CPU Jobs for reading engine source. When a flag was undocumented, the agent ran a cheap cpu-upgrade Job to grep the installed Python package inside the container. That is how it found SGLang's SGLANG_OPT_* environment variables and vLLM's speculative-config fields. Inference Endpoints for deployment, created via hf endpoints deploy using the exact image digest and flags that passed verification. The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding. Results Single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate. Config (1× RTX PRO 6000) 1-user decode (tok/s) 8-user aggregate (tok/s) Prefill 4K / 32K (tok/s) TTFT SGLang, no speculation (baseline) 134–139 543–598 18.7–19.1K / 16.9–19.1K 41–114 ms vLLM, no speculation 157.0 638 20.7K / 20.7K 33 ms SGLang + DSpark (8 drafts) 166.6 — ¹ 18.0–19.5K / 18.9–19.1K 38–51 ms vLLM + DSpark (7 drafts) 190.6 716 20.7K / 20.6K 40 ms Deployed endpoint (over the internet) 194.9 673 11.7K / 19.2K ² 198 ms ² ¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip. All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB: vllm serve thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini \ --tool-call-parser inkling \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --reasoning-parser inkling \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work ). Why it stops around 190 tok/s Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job ( 1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s . Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits. Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s . At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth , so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer. What didn't work Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower: vLLM Lever Result Shorter draft length (3–6) Rejected at startup; requires num_speculative_tokens = 7 (checkpoint block size − 1). draft_sample_method: "greedy" −11% at temperature 1.0 (168.6 vs ~190.4 tok/s). rejection_sample_method: "block" 190.1 vs 190.3–190.5 for controls; no effect. enable_adaptive_verification Assertion error at startup for the Inkling 2 drafter. draft_lm_head_quantization: "fp8" Only supported for DeepSeek DSpark drafters. We also skipped rejection_sample_method: "fly" and "synthetic" on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup. SGLang Lever Result Shorter draft length (3–6) Rejected at startup; requires --speculative-num-draft-tokens 8 ( gamma + 1 for the bundled drafter). SGLANG_ENABLE_NV_MEGA_RUNTIME_OPTIMIZATION=1 +4% once, failed to reproduce against fresh controls. SGLANG_OPT_USE_FUSED_DRAFT_SAMPLE=1 +2%, within run-to-run noise. SGLANG_OPT_MOE_QUANT_ONCE=1 +1%, within run-to-run noise. SGLANG_DSPARK_USE_GREEDY_DRAFT=1 −9% at temperature 1.0 (156.8 vs ~172 tok/s). Benchmarking gotchas A few measurement issues caught us along the way: Triton JIT during timed prefill. vLLM's first 4K prefill came back at 202 tok/s instead of 20K because Triton was compiling kernels during the timed request. Running an unmeasured warmup across prompt lengths and concurrency fixed 4K prefill, though the first run in each Job still under-reported 32K prefill due to last-chunk shape differences (flagged in the ledger). Orphaned servers holding GPU memory. The initial driver stopped servers via a PID saved from setsid … & , which is not guaranteed to match the process group ID. The previous server stayed alive on port 8000, broke the next launch, and turned into a zombie that still passed kill -0 . Managing the process with subprocess.Popen(start_new_session=True) and waiting until both GPU memory and port 8000 are free fixed it. Hidden OOM errors in vLLM logs. vLLM + DSpark twice died with "Engine core initialization failed" at the end of the log while the real causes sat 200 lines up. First, the default 1M-token KV cache needed 52.6 GiB with only 48.1 GiB free alongside the drafter ( --max-model-len 262144 fixed this). Next, because vLLM v0.34.0 raised the default --gpu-memory-utilization from 0.92 to 1.0 , the KV cache claimed the remaining VRAM and OOMed the drafter's 5 GiB allocation ( --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 fixed this). The driver now prints every error line from the server log instead of just the tail. Engine variance. Across identical runs with speculation, vLLM stayed within 0.4% while SGLang swung by ±4.5%. That was wide enough to make SGLANG_ENABLE_NV_MEGA_RUNTIME_OPTIMIZATION=1 look like a +4% win on its first run before repeat controls ruled it out. Verification and deployment Before deploying, we pinned the exact vLLM nightly digest ( vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6… , build 0.34.0rc1.dev1235+gf2f9edcac ) and ran the acceptance gates inside a Job: Gate Result Needle retrieval at ~50% context (126,537 tokens) 3/3, TTFT 12.5 s Needle retrieval at ~95% context (249,970 tokens) 3/3, TTFT 28.7 s Concurrent soak (4 × ~58K-token requests) 4/4 succeeded, 3/3 retrieval each Greedy equivalence, DSpark vs no speculation (6 prompts, temp 0) 6/6 byte-identical Single-user decode on pinned image 189.9 / 190.2 tok/s Once those passed, we deployed the endpoint with a single hf endpoints deploy command, pinning both the image digest and model revision (authenticated access, scale-to-zero after 60 idle minutes): hf endpoints deploy inkling2mini-tuned-dspark --namespace \ --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --revision 7a67ae2314b44ef05c87fd1d4d311c58aaeb18f6 \ --framework custom --custom-image "vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6ee3aac77f3158e80ed79ec425db3a53f7cd666bf1954e96abfaf19a7" \ --health-route /health --port 8000 \ --vendor aws --region us-east-2 --accelerator gpu --instance-type nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 --instance-size x1 \ --min-replica 0 --max-replica 1 --scale-to-zero-timeout 60 -- type authenticated \ --container-command "vllm serve" \ --container-args "/repository --served-model-name thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --tool-call-parser inkling --enable-auto-tool-choice --reasoning-parser inkling --max-model-len 262144 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --speculative-config '{\"method\":\"dspark\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":7,\"draft_sample_method\":\"probabilistic\"}'" Running bench.py against the live endpoint gave 194.9 tok/s single-user, matching the Job runs once network latency is accounted for. Everything from this run ( PLAN.md , THEORY.md , jobs/driver.py , submit.sh , deploy.sh , and the raw ledger-*.jsonl files) is in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb . To reuse the loop on another model, put your candidate and control server commands into a configs/plan-*.json file and submit it to whichever HF Jobs GPU flavor matches your target endpoint. Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Where scientists draw the line on AI agents Enterprise Article Published November 25, 2026 Upvote 9 +3 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai :last-child]:mb-0"> 📄 Tech Report Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work. These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings. To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies. Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used. One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust : validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research. Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized. A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge. Helping researchers check the work For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually. But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs. Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis. But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way. Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows. These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks. These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like. Keep scientific judgment in the loop Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process? An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?” Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves. Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation. Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said. Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research. These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work. The same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Meanwhile, participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used. Both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry. This is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work. Build AI agents alongside scientists Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology. Researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities. It will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify important concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science. Still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it. The promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.
